rv.q: Jammed with ideas, rich with humanity, Consent is a modern classic.
This is a vivid, thoughtful and immensely resonant play and Roger Michell’s deft, subtly acted production keeps you gripped throughout.
This bracingly clever, bleakly funny play offers no easy answers to any of its questions: what is justice, what is vengeance, and which is right?

Roger Michell’s superbly performed, almost fully recast production (saving Heather Craney as the let-down rape-victim and Adam James as amiable-arrogant Jake) handles the volatile mixture of light and shade with supreme finesse.
As philandering Jake, Adam James's shift between his gung-ho social self and deflation in the aftermath of eviction by his wife Rachel (a suitably tense Sian Clifford) is masterly.
Miss Raine skilfully creates a world in which everything has more than one side.
But Roger Michell’s production feels less substantial on the West End stage, narrower in world view, more conservative in form and, for a play that’s only a year old, strangely dated.
'Consent' is so bold, so far-reaching that it's a shame to see it ultimately subside into something so safe and so in thrall to the status quo.
Few have managed to dramatise the judicious and the judgmental with such exhilarating elan.
In fact, its vivid complexity is one of the qualities that makes Consent such an unmissable play.
It demonstrates, with a wounding intensity, just how much it costs each of the parties.

The glib one-liners, caustic barbs and politically incorrect asides, fit neatly into the comfortable, professional, middle-class environment and lend great comic strength to a play which is inherently filled with emotional angst and heartbreak - every ounce of which, has been drawn-out by Roger Michell's provocative direction.
The play fizzles out and doesn’t tackle the central drama effectively.
Consent is an addictive and thought-provoking play, but I can’t think of a worse place for a barrister to bring a date.
An impressive cast and excellent dialogue feature in Consent, but as the plot develops, some of the production’s underlying points get lost along the way.
The second half almost completely drops one of the three main storylines, leaving the theatre-goers perplexed with regards to the central narrative.

cn.t: Raine's sharp, darkly comic drama about lawyers navigating rape cases and marital betrayals earns strong praise for its intelligent writing and timely relevance, though some find its privileged characters problematic.
